timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: I use a VPN to stay safe online. That makes me unhackable, right?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Not even close, Peter. A VPN encrypts your traffic between you and the VPN server. But after that, it travels normally. And the VPN provider itself can see everything - so you're just shifting trust from your ISP to the VPN company.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Wait, the VPN can see my traffic?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Yes. They're the endpoint of the encrypted tunnel. If they log your activity, your protection is an illusion. That's why no-log VPN policies matter - and why you need to verify them through independent audits.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Protocol choice matters enormously. WireGuard is modern, fast, and secure but has a small codebase that's easier to audit. OpenVPN is mature but complex. IPsec is built into the OS but has had implementation vulnerabilities.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: If you're not paying, you're the product. Free VPNs log and sell your data, inject ads, or worse - some have been found injecting malware. The 2020 UFO VPN breach exposed 1.2 billion user records. Always use a reputable, audited, paid VPN.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Enterprise VPNs are a different beast. Pulse Secure, Fortinet, and Citrix VPN gateways have been high-value targets for APT groups. The 2020 Pulse Secure exploit let attackers read credentials directly from memory.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Should I use a VPN for everything?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: It depends. On public WiFi, absolutely. At home, it adds a layer but your ISP already sees your traffic. For bypassing geo-restrictions, yes. For actual security, combine VPN with DNS over HTTPS, a firewall, and good browser security.
